The third integrative exercise asks why the highest poles do not depend on the scheme. It combines
@exm-ren-2l-double-pole with @prp-ren-scheme-independence.

::: {#exr-ren-x-highest-pole}
#### Highest poles are universal

Show that in any scheme in which the counterterms are $\lambda_0\mu^{-\epsilon} = \lambda + \sum_ka_k(\lambda)\epsilon^{-k}$ with $a_k = O(\lambda^{k + 1})$, the leading
coefficient $[\lambda^{k + 1}]a_k = b_1^k$, where $b_1$ is the one-loop coefficient. Why does this make $b_1$ scheme independent from a
second point of view?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
By @exr-ren-2l-double-pole, $\lambda a_{k + 1}' - a_{k + 1} = \hat\beta a_k'$. With $a_k = \alpha_k\lambda^{k + 1} + \dots$ and $\hat\beta = b_1\lambda^2 + \dots$, the leading terms give $(k + 1)\alpha_{k + 1}
= b_1(k + 1)\alpha_k$, so $\alpha_{k + 1} = b_1\alpha_k$ and $\alpha_k = b_1^k$ since $\alpha_1 = b_1$. A finite renormalisation $\lambda \to \lambda + c\lambda^2$ changes $a_k$ only at
orders $\lambda^{k + 2}$ and beyond, so the leading poles are the same in every scheme with these properties, and with them
$b_1 = \alpha_1$; this is the content of @balduf2024dyson [Thm. 58, items 1-2].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

## BPHZ and forests {#sec-bphz}

At two loops the counterterm graphs of @sec-renormalised-perturbation removed the non-local poles, and the overall
divergence that remained was local. To all orders the bookkeeping becomes intricate: subdivergences sit inside
subdivergences, and some overlap. Bogoliubov and Parasiuk gave a recursive subtraction, Hepp proved that it works, and
Zimmermann solved the recursion in closed form as a sum over **forests**, sets of non-overlapping divergent subgraphs.
Connes and Kreimer later recognised the combinatorics as that of a Hopf algebra, in which the counterterm of a graph is
a twisted antipode [@balduf2024dyson, Secs. 2.2 and 2.3.4].

### Forests

The subtraction operator $T_\gamma$ acting on a subgraph replaces its integrand by the part that produces its divergence: in
momentum subtraction the Taylor polynomial of degree $\omega(\gamma)$ in its external momenta at a reference point, in minimal
subtraction the pole part $K$ of its regularised value. The figure shows the three two-loop graphs of the quartic theory
with their subdivergences, and the number of forests of each.

![The subdivergences of the two-loop graphs of the quartic theory, shaded. Left: the chain of two bubbles, which share a
vertex and therefore overlap; $6$ forests. Middle: the eye graph, with one bubble nested inside the whole graph; $4$
forests. Right: the sunset, whose three subdivergences (pairs of lines) overlap pairwise; $8$ forests. The whole graph,
superficially divergent in each case, belongs to half of the forests. Generated by
`figures/ren-forests.sage`.](figures/ren-forests.svg){#fig-ren-forests width=95%}

The definition fixes what may appear together in a subtraction term. Two subgraphs may be subtracted in one term only if
one contains the other or they do not touch.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-ren-forest}
#### Forest

Let $\Gamma$ be a one-particle-irreducible graph and $\mathcal D(\Gamma)$ the set of its one-particle-irreducible subgraphs $\gamma$ with $\omega(\gamma) \geq 0$,
$\Gamma$ itself included if it is superficially divergent. Two subgraphs **overlap** if they share a vertex or a line and
neither contains the other. A **forest** of $\Gamma$ is a subset $F \subseteq \mathcal D(\Gamma)$, the empty set included, no two elements of which
overlap. The **forest formula** of Zimmermann assigns to $\Gamma$ the renormalised integrand
$$
R\,I_\Gamma = \sum_F\prod_{\gamma \in F}(-T_\gamma)\,I_\Gamma ,
$$ {#eq-ren-forest-formula}
where in each product the operators act from the smallest subgraph outwards and $T_\gamma$ acts on the integrand of $\gamma$ with
the inner subtractions already made.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
At one loop there are no subdivergences, and the formula is a single subtraction. The first example writes it out for
the bubble.

::: {#exm-ren-forest-one-loop}
#### One loop

The bubble $\Gamma$ has $\mathcal D(\Gamma) = \{\Gamma\}$ and the forests $\emptyset$ and $\{\Gamma\}$, so $R\,I_\Gamma = (1 - T_\Gamma)I_\Gamma$. With momentum subtraction at zero
momentum, $T_\Gamma I_\Gamma(p) = I_\Gamma(0)$, and $R\,I_\Gamma = I_\Gamma(p) - I_\Gamma(0)$ is the subtracted bubble of @exm-ren-pv-subtracted, finite before any
regulator is introduced: the subtraction can be done under the integral sign, $\int d^4\ell\,(\frac{1}{(\ell^2 + m^2)((\ell + p)^2 + m^2)} -
\frac{1}{(\ell^2 + m^2)^2})$, whose integrand falls like $\ell^{-5}$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A nested subdivergence gives a product of two subtractions, applied from the inside out. The second example is the
eye graph of @exm-ren-2l-eye.

::: {#exm-ren-forest-eye}
#### The eye graph

The eye graph has $\mathcal D = \{\gamma, \Gamma\}$ with the inner bubble $\gamma \subset \Gamma$. Its forests are $\emptyset$, $\{\gamma\}$, $\{\Gamma\}$ and $\{\gamma, \Gamma\}$, and
@eq-ren-forest-formula gives
$$
R\,I_\Gamma = I_\Gamma - T_\gamma I_\Gamma - T_\Gamma I_\Gamma + T_\Gamma T_\gamma I_\Gamma = (1 - T_\Gamma)(1 - T_\gamma)I_\Gamma .
$$
The second term is the counterterm graph of @exm-ren-2l-eye, and the last two together are the overall counterterm of
$\Gamma$ evaluated on the graph with its subdivergence already subtracted, $-T_\Gamma\bar R\,I_\Gamma$ with $\bar R = 1 - T_\gamma$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

When two subdivergences overlap they never appear in the same forest. The third example is the chain, whose two
bubbles share a vertex.

::: {#exm-ren-forest-chain}
#### The chain

The chain has $\mathcal D = \{\gamma_1, \gamma_2, \Gamma\}$, and $\gamma_1$, $\gamma_2$ share the middle vertex. The forests are $\emptyset$, $\{\gamma_1\}$, $\{\gamma_2\}$, $\{\Gamma\}$,
$\{\gamma_1, \Gamma\}$ and $\{\gamma_2, \Gamma\}$, six of them, and
$$
R\,I_\Gamma = (1 - T_\Gamma)(1 - T_{\gamma_1} - T_{\gamma_2})I_\Gamma .
$$
With minimal subtraction this is $B^2 - 2K(B)B - K(B^2 - 2K(B)B)$, whose pole part vanishes by @exm-ren-2l-chain. The product
$T_{\gamma_1}T_{\gamma_2}$ does not occur: contracting both bubbles would merge three vertices into one, which no counterterm
provides.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The sunset has three subdivergences, each overlapping the other two. The fourth example counts its forests and shows
that the overall subtraction must remove two powers of momentum.

::: {#exm-ren-forest-sunset}
#### The sunset

Each pair of the three lines of the sunset forms a four-point subgraph $\gamma_i$ with $\omega = 0$; the sunset itself has $\omega = 2$.
Since the $\gamma_i$ overlap, the forests are $\emptyset$, $\{\gamma_i\}$, $\{\Gamma\}$ and $\{\gamma_i, \Gamma\}$, eight in all, and $R\,I_\Gamma = (1 - T_\Gamma)(1 - T_{\gamma_1} -
T_{\gamma_2} - T_{\gamma_3})I_\Gamma$. In momentum subtraction $T_\Gamma$ is the Taylor polynomial of degree two in the external momentum, $I(0) +
\frac12p^\mu p^\nu\partial_\mu\partial_\nu I(0)$, whose two terms are a mass and a field-strength counterterm (@exm-ren-2l-sunset).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The exercises count forests by computer, apply the Taylor operator, and evaluate a renormalised two-loop graph. The
first counts the forests of a chain of bubbles.

::: {#exr-ren-forest-count}
#### Forests of a chain

In the $s$-channel chain of $n$ bubbles, the divergent subgraphs are the runs of consecutive bubbles $[i, j]$, $1 \leq i \leq j \leq
n$, and two runs overlap unless one contains the other or there is at least one bubble between them. Count the forests
for $n = 1, \dots, 6$ with Sage.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Two runs $[i, j]$ and $[k, l]$ with $j < k$ share a vertex when $k = j + 1$, so they are compatible only if $k \geq j + 2$ or they
are nested. Enumerating all subsets of the $n(n + 1)/2$ runs, the numbers of forests are $2, 6, 22, 90, 394, 1806$ for $n =
1, \dots, 6$, the large Schröder numbers: the same numbers count the ways to bracket a sequence, which is what a
forest of runs does:

{{< sage exr-ren-forest-count >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The Taylor operator of momentum subtraction acts on the integrand, before integration. The second exercise applies it to
the sunset.

::: {#exr-ren-forest-taylor}
#### The Taylor operator on the sunset

For the Euclidean sunset $I(p) = \int\int\frac{d^4k\,d^4l}{(2\pi)^8}\frac{1}{(k^2 + m^2)(l^2 + m^2)((p - k - l)^2 + m^2)}$, write $T_\Gamma I$ with the Taylor
polynomial of degree two at $p = 0$, show that its $p$-dependent part is proportional to $p^2$ by rotation invariance,
and identify the counterterms it represents.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$T_\Gamma I(p) = I(0) + p^\mu\partial_\mu I(0) + \frac12p^\mu p^\nu\partial_\mu\partial_\nu I(0)$. The linear term vanishes because $\partial_\mu I(0)$ is a vector built from
no external vector; the quadratic term is $\frac12p^\mu p^\nu\frac{\delta_{\mu\nu}}{4}\partial^2I(0) = \frac{p^2}{8}\partial^2I(0)$. The constant $I(0)$ is a mass
counterterm ($\delta_m$) and the $p^2$ term a field counterterm ($\delta_Z$); these are the only two operators of dimension at most
four with two fields, as power counting requires.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The renormalised eye graph must be finite when the regulator is removed. The third exercise checks this with the
integrals of @exr-ren-2l-eye.

::: {#exr-ren-forest-eye-finite}
#### The renormalised eye graph

With the eye graph and the bubble of @exr-ren-2l-eye in minimal subtraction, compute $R = (1 - K)(\text{eye} - K(B)B)$ with Sage,
show that it is finite as $\epsilon \to 0$, and find its dependence on $L = \log(p^2/\mu^2)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The subtracted combination $\text{eye} - \frac2\epsilon B$ has the local poles $-\frac2{\epsilon^2} + \frac1\epsilon$; removing them leaves the finite part, a polynomial
of degree two in $L$, $\frac{L^2}{2} - 3L + \frac{11}{2}$ in units of $(16\pi^2)^{-2}$. The leading coefficient $\frac12$ is that of
the leading logarithm, and the coefficient of $L$ is fixed by the one-loop poles, as the renormalisation group requires:

{{< sage exr-ren-forest-eye-finite >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The forest formula is a theorem only because the sum over forests is finite after integration. The theorem states
this, in the form in which it is usually proved.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#thm-ren-bphz}
#### The BPHZ theorem

In a theory renormalisable by power counting, for every one-particle-irreducible graph $\Gamma$ the forest formula
@eq-ren-forest-formula with momentum subtraction produces an absolutely convergent integral, and with dimensional
regularisation and minimal subtraction a finite limit as $\epsilon \to 0$. The terms with $\Gamma \in F$ are local, polynomials in the
external momenta of degree $\omega(\Gamma)$, and the sum of the terms with $\Gamma \notin F$ is the sum of $\Gamma$ and its counterterm graphs; so
the forest formula is the same as adding local counterterms to the Lagrangian order by order [@balduf2024dyson, Thm.
34 and the remarks after it].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The theorem identifies the forests with counterterm graphs, which is what makes it a statement about Lagrangians. The
first example makes the identification explicit at two loops.

::: {#exm-ren-bphz-counterterms}
#### Forests are counterterm graphs

For the eye graph, the forest $\{\gamma\}$ gives $-T_\gamma I_\Gamma = -T_\gamma I_\gamma\cdot I_{\Gamma/\gamma}$, the counterterm $-\delta_\lambda^{(1)}$ of the inner bubble inserted as
a vertex in the outer bubble; the forests $\{\Gamma\}$ and $\{\gamma, \Gamma\}$ give $-T_\Gamma(I_\Gamma - T_\gamma I_\Gamma)$, the contribution of $\Gamma$ to the two-loop
counterterm $\delta_\lambda^{(2)}$. Summing over all two-loop graphs, the forests containing the whole graph produce
$\delta_\lambda^{(2)}$, $\delta_m^{(2)}$ and $\delta_Z^{(2)}$, the coefficients of the Lagrangian counterterms of @def-ren-counterterm.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The choice of subtraction operator is a choice of scheme. The second example compares momentum subtraction with
minimal subtraction in the forest formula.

::: {#exm-ren-bphz-schemes}
#### Two subtraction operators

With $T_\gamma$ the Taylor polynomial at zero external momenta the forest formula needs no regulator at all, since it
subtracts under the integral sign; this is BPHZ in its original form and requires masses, or a non-zero subtraction
point, to avoid infrared divergences. With $T_\gamma = K$, the pole part after dimensional regularisation, it is the
minimal scheme. Both satisfy the condition that makes the counterterms multiplicative, the Rota-Baxter property of the
subtraction (@exr-ren-hopf-rota-baxter).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Overlapping divergences were the historical obstacle to a proof. The third example explains why the forest formula
handles them without special treatment.

::: {#exm-ren-bphz-overlapping}
#### Overlapping divergences

In the sunset, each $\gamma_i$ diverges in the region where its two loop momenta grow while the third line stays fixed. The
forests $\{\gamma_i\}$ remove these regions one at a time, and no forest subtracts two of them at once, because the regions
where two pairs of lines are hard together are regions where all three are, the overall divergence handled by
$\{\Gamma\}$ and $\{\gamma_i, \Gamma\}$. Hepp's proof divides the integration domain into sectors in which the momenta are ordered, and in
each sector only nested subgraphs become large, so overlapping graphs never need to be subtracted together.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The exercises check the algebra of the forest formula on nested subgraphs, show that the overall subtraction is
local, and relate the formula to the recursion of Bogoliubov. The first is an identity.

::: {#exr-ren-bphz-nested}
#### Nested subtractions factorise

For a chain of nested subgraphs $\gamma_1 \subset \gamma_2 \subset \dots \subset \gamma_k = \Gamma$ with no other divergent subgraphs, show that the forest formula
is $R = (1 - T_{\gamma_k})\cdots(1 - T_{\gamma_1})$ and count its terms.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Any two elements of the chain are nested, so every subset of $\{\gamma_1, \dots, \gamma_k\}$ is a forest: there are $2^k$ forests. The term for
a subset $F$ is $\prod_{\gamma \in F}(-T_\gamma)$ in the order from inside out, which is exactly the term with the factors $-T_{\gamma_j}$, $\gamma_j \in F$,
selected from the expanded product $(1 - T_{\gamma_k})\cdots(1 - T_{\gamma_1})$. The product has $2^k$ terms, one for each forest.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The overall subtraction of a graph must be a polynomial in its external momenta, otherwise it could not be a term of a
Lagrangian. The second exercise shows why, for momentum subtraction.

::: {#exr-ren-bphz-local}
#### The overall subtraction is local

Let $\bar R\,I_\Gamma$ be the integrand of $\Gamma$ with all its proper subdivergences subtracted. Show that $T_\Gamma\bar R\,I_\Gamma$ is a
polynomial of degree $\omega(\Gamma)$ in the external momenta, and that differentiating $\bar R\,I_\Gamma$ $\omega(\Gamma) + 1$ times with respect to them gives a
convergent integral.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$T_\Gamma$ is by definition the Taylor polynomial of degree $\omega(\Gamma)$ at zero external momenta, a polynomial whose coefficients
are integrals over loop momenta alone. Each derivative with respect to an external momentum acts on a propagator,
$\partial_p\frac{1}{(k + p)^2 + m^2} = -\frac{2(k + p)}{((k + p)^2 + m^2)^2}$, and lowers the degree of divergence of every subgraph containing that line by
one. After $\omega(\Gamma) + 1$ derivatives the overall degree is $-1$, and the subgraphs, already subtracted in $\bar R$, stay
convergent: by Weinberg's theorem the integral converges. So the divergence of $\bar R\,I_\Gamma$ sits entirely in its Taylor
coefficients of order at most $\omega(\Gamma)$, which $T_\Gamma$ removes.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Bogoliubov's original recursion defines the counterterm of a graph through the counterterms of its subgraphs. The third
exercise relates it to the forest formula.

::: {#exr-ren-bphz-bogoliubov}
#### Bogoliubov's recursion

Define $\bar R\,I_\Gamma = I_\Gamma + \sum_{\{\gamma_1, \dots, \gamma_r\}}\prod_iC(\gamma_i)\,I_{\Gamma/\{\gamma_i\}}$, the sum over sets of pairwise vertex-disjoint proper subdivergences, with
$C(\gamma) = -T_\gamma\bar R\,I_\gamma$, and $R\,I_\Gamma = (1 - T_\Gamma)\bar R\,I_\Gamma$. Show that for the eye graph and the chain this reproduces
@exm-ren-forest-eye and @exm-ren-forest-chain.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
For the eye graph the only proper subdivergence is $\gamma$, with $C(\gamma) = -T_\gamma I_\gamma$ (no subdivergences of its own), so $\bar R\,I_\Gamma =
I_\Gamma - T_\gamma I_\gamma I_{\Gamma/\gamma}$ and $R = (1 - T_\Gamma)(1 - T_\gamma)I_\Gamma$. For the chain the sets are $\{\gamma_1\}$ and $\{\gamma_2\}$ ($\{\gamma_1, \gamma_2\}$ is excluded because they
share a vertex), so $\bar R\,I_\Gamma = I_\Gamma - T_{\gamma_1}I_\Gamma - T_{\gamma_2}I_\Gamma$, and $R = (1 - T_\Gamma)\bar R$. In general, expanding the recursion produces each
forest once; Zimmermann's formula is its solution.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

### The Hopf algebra of renormalisation

The recursion of Bogoliubov has the form of an antipode in a Hopf algebra. Graphs are multiplied by disjoint union,
and the coproduct of a graph lists its divergent subgraphs together with the graphs obtained by contracting them; the
counterterm is then a twisted antipode, and renormalised Feynman rules are a convolution product
[@balduf2024dyson, Secs. 2.1.3-2.1.5 and 2.2.3-2.2.4]. A toy model with one-dimensional integrals shows the structure
without the integrals of field theory, and the figure shows its renormalised amplitudes.

![The toy model of @balduf2024dyson [Example 80], $F[B_+(t)](s) = \int_0^\infty dx\frac{x^{-\epsilon}}{x + s}F[t](x)$, renormalised by subtraction at $s = 1$.
The renormalised amplitudes of the bamboo trees $b_1$, $b_2$, $b_3$, $b_4$ (one, two, three and four nested loops) at $\epsilon = 0$, as
functions of $L = \log s$: $-L$, $\frac{L^2}{2}$, $-\frac{L^3}{6} - \frac{\pi^2L}{6}$, $\frac{L^4}{24} + \frac{\pi^2L^2}{6}$. The leading powers $\frac{(-L)^n}{n!}$ are the leading logarithms; the
$\pi^2$ terms come from the expansion of the one-loop kernel. Generated by `figures/ren-toy-model.sage`.](figures/ren-toy-model.svg){#fig-ren-toy-model width=70%}

The definition states the coproduct and the counterterm it defines. The renormalised Feynman rules follow from them in
one line.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-ren-coproduct}
#### Coproduct of Feynman graphs

The **Hopf algebra of Feynman graphs** is the vector space spanned by graphs, with the product given by disjoint
union and the empty graph as unit. Its **coproduct** is
$$
\Delta(\Gamma) = \Gamma \otimes 1 + 1 \otimes \Gamma + \sum_{\gamma}\gamma \otimes \Gamma/\gamma ,
$$
the sum running over the proper subgraphs $\gamma$ that are products of vertex-disjoint one-particle-irreducible
superficially divergent graphs with at least one loop, and $\Gamma/\gamma$ the graph with each component of $\gamma$ contracted to a vertex
[@balduf2024dyson, Def. 86]. A graph is **primitive** if the sum is empty. Given Feynman rules $F$ and a subtraction
$R$, the **counterterm** is defined recursively by $S_R(\Gamma) = -R\bigl[F(\Gamma) + \sum_\gamma S_R(\gamma)F(\Gamma/\gamma)\bigr]$, and the renormalised Feynman
rules are $F_R(\Gamma) = F(\Gamma) + \sum_\gamma S_R(\gamma)F(\Gamma/\gamma) + S_R(\Gamma)$ [@balduf2024dyson, Defs. 90-91].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
All one-loop graphs are primitive, and their renormalisation is the subtraction of @exm-ren-forest-one-loop. The first
example writes the formulas for them.

::: {#exm-ren-hopf-primitive}
#### Primitive graphs

For the bubble $b$, $\Delta(b) = b \otimes 1 + 1 \otimes b$, $S_R(b) = -R F(b)$ and $F_R(b) = (1 - R)F(b)$. With minimal subtraction $S_R(b) = -\frac{2}{16\pi^2\epsilon}$
in the units where the vertex factor is one, the counterterm $\delta_\lambda^{(1)}$ per channel. A graph with several loops can also be
primitive, if none of its proper subgraphs diverges: in the quartic theory there is no primitive four-point graph at
two loops and one at three loops [@kompaniets2017minimally, Table I; @balduf2024dyson, Example 73].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The coproduct of the eye graph has one middle term. The second example computes its counterterm and finds the
expression of @exm-ren-forest-eye.

::: {#exm-ren-hopf-eye}
#### The eye graph in the Hopf algebra

$\Delta(\Gamma) = \Gamma \otimes 1 + 1 \otimes \Gamma + \gamma \otimes \Gamma/\gamma$, where $\gamma$ is the inner bubble and $\Gamma/\gamma$ the outer bubble with a vertex in its place.
The counterterm is $S_R(\Gamma) = -R[F(\Gamma) + S_R(\gamma)F(\Gamma/\gamma)] = -R[F(\Gamma) - R F(\gamma)F(\Gamma/\gamma)]$, and $F_R(\Gamma) = (1 - R)[F(\Gamma) - RF(\gamma)F(\Gamma/\gamma)]$: the
forest formula of the eye graph, with nested subtractions written as an iterated $R$. This is @balduf2024dyson [Example
81] for the analogous graph of the cubic theory, the dunce's cap.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

For the chain the coproduct contains the same term twice and nothing with both bubbles. The third example shows why,
and the counterterm that results.

::: {#exm-ren-hopf-chain}
#### The chain in the Hopf algebra

The two bubbles of the chain share a vertex, so their union is not a product of vertex-disjoint graphs and does not
appear in $\Delta$: $\Delta(\Gamma) = \Gamma \otimes 1 + 1 \otimes \Gamma + 2\,b \otimes b$, since contracting either bubble leaves a bubble. Then $S_R(\Gamma) = -R[F(\Gamma) +
2S_R(b)F(b)] = -R[B^2 - 2R(B)B]$, the counterterm of @exm-ren-2l-chain, and in minimal subtraction it is $\frac{4}{(16\pi^2)^2\epsilon^2}$ with
no simple pole.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The essential combinatorics is already present in rooted trees, which record only the nesting of subgraphs. The
fourth example computes the coproduct and antipode of the smallest trees, the Hopf algebra of Connes and Kreimer.

::: {#exm-ren-hopf-trees}
#### Rooted trees

A rooted tree stands for a graph whose subdivergences are nested as the tree says: $\bullet$ for a primitive graph, the
bamboo $b_2$ (two vertices, one above the other) for a graph with one subdivergence. Admissible cuts give $\Delta(\bullet) = \bullet \otimes 1 +
1 \otimes \bullet$ and $\Delta(b_2) = b_2 \otimes 1 + 1 \otimes b_2 + \bullet \otimes \bullet$, and the antipode, defined by $S(\Gamma) = -\Gamma - \sum S(\gamma)\Gamma/\gamma$, is $S(\bullet) = -\bullet$, $S(b_2) =
-b_2 + \bullet\bullet$ [@balduf2024dyson, Example 76]. The eye graph maps to $b_2$; the chain maps to $b_2$ as well, with the coefficient $2$
of its middle term recording the two ways of choosing the inner bubble.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The exercises renormalise the toy model, compute antipodes, and test the property of the subtraction that makes the
counterterms multiplicative. The first is a Sage computation.

::: {#exr-ren-hopf-toy}
#### The toy model

In the toy model of @fig-ren-toy-model, $F[b_n](s) = s^{-n\epsilon}\prod_{j = 1}^n\frac{\pi}{\sin\pi j\epsilon}$ for the bamboo $b_n$. With $R$ the evaluation at $s = 1$,
compute $S_R(b_n)$ and $F_R[b_n]$ for $n = 1, \dots, 4$ with Sage, using $\Delta(b_n) = \sum_{k = 0}^nb_k \otimes b_{n - k}$, and take $\epsilon \to 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$F[B_+(x^{-k\epsilon})](s) = \int_0^\infty\frac{x^{-(k + 1)\epsilon}}{x + s}dx = \frac{\pi}{\sin\pi(k + 1)\epsilon}s^{-(k + 1)\epsilon}$, which gives $F[b_n]$ by induction. The recursion
$S_R(b_n) = -R[F(b_n) + \sum_{k = 1}^{n - 1}S_R(b_k)F(b_{n - k})]$ and $F_R(b_n) = F(b_n) + \sum_{k = 1}^{n - 1}S_R(b_k)F(b_{n - k}) + S_R(b_n)$ give, as $\epsilon \to 0$, $F_R(b_1) =
-L$, $F_R(b_2) = \frac{L^2}{2}$, $F_R(b_3) = -\frac{L^3}{6} - \frac{\pi^2}{6}L$ and $F_R(b_4) = \frac{L^4}{24} + \frac{\pi^2}{6}L^2$; all poles cancel:

{{< sage exr-ren-hopf-toy >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The antipode of the Connes-Kreimer algebra can be computed by hand for small trees. The second exercise does it for the
two trees with three vertices.

::: {#exr-ren-hopf-antipode}
#### Antipodes of trees with three vertices

For the bamboo $b_3$ and the tree $c$ with a root and two leaves, the admissible cuts give $\Delta(b_3) = b_3 \otimes 1 + 1 \otimes b_3 + \bullet \otimes
b_2 + b_2 \otimes \bullet$ and $\Delta(c) = c \otimes 1 + 1 \otimes c + 2\,\bullet \otimes b_2 + \bullet\bullet \otimes \bullet$. Compute $S(b_3)$ and $S(c)$, and check $m(S \otimes \mathrm{id})\Delta = 0$
on both.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$S(b_3) = -b_3 - S(\bullet)b_2 - S(b_2)\bullet = -b_3 + \bullet b_2 + b_2\bullet - \bullet\bullet\bullet = -b_3 + 2\bullet b_2 - \bullet^3$. $S(c) = -c - 2S(\bullet)b_2 - S(\bullet\bullet)\bullet =
-c + 2\bullet b_2 - \bullet^3$, using $S(\bullet\bullet) = S(\bullet)^2 = \bullet\bullet$. Check for $c$: $m(S \otimes \mathrm{id})\Delta(c) = S(c) + c + 2S(\bullet)b_2 + S(\bullet\bullet)\bullet = (-c + 2\bullet b_2 - \bullet^3) + c - 2\bullet b_2 +
\bullet^3 = 0$, and similarly for $b_3$. The two trees have the same antipode up to the tree itself, a reflection of the fact
that in both the overall divergence sees one primitive inside another twice.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The counterterm is a character, multiplicative on disjoint unions, only if the subtraction satisfies the Rota-Baxter
identity $R(fg) + R(f)R(g) = R(R(f)g) + R(fR(g))$ [@balduf2024dyson, eq. 2.39]. The third exercise tests it.

::: {#exr-ren-hopf-rota-baxter}
#### The Rota-Baxter identity

Check with Sage that the pole-part projection $K$ on Laurent polynomials in $\epsilon$ and the evaluation $R_{s_0}f(s) = f(s_0)$ satisfy
the Rota-Baxter identity on random examples, and that the operator "keep the $\epsilon^0$ term" does not.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
For $K$, write $f = f_- + f_+$ (poles and the rest), so $K(f) = f_-$. Expanding $fg$ in the four products, $K(f_-g_-) = f_-g_-$ and
$K(f_+g_+) = 0$, and all terms of $K(fg) + f_-g_- - K(f_-g) - K(fg_-)$ cancel. For the evaluation, $R(R(f)g) = f(s_0)g(s_0) = R(f)R(g)$ and the
identity reads $2R(f)R(g) = R(fg) + R(f)R(g)$, true since $R(fg) = R(f)R(g)$. The projection on the $\epsilon^0$ term is not a
Rota-Baxter operator, and with it the counterterms of disjoint graphs would not multiply:

{{< sage exr-ren-hopf-rota-baxter >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

### Exercises

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first integrative exercise combines the forests of the sunset with power counting. It asks for the complete
renormalised integrand.

::: {#exr-ren-x-sunset-forests}
#### The sunset renormalised

Write the forest formula for the massive sunset with momentum subtraction at $p = 0$, specify the degree of each Taylor
operator, and count how many independent integrals the eight forests produce after using rotation invariance.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$R = (1 - T^{(2)}_\Gamma)(1 - T^{(0)}_{\gamma_1} - T^{(0)}_{\gamma_2} - T^{(0)}_{\gamma_3})I_\Gamma$, with $T^{(0)}_{\gamma_i}$ the value of the bubble $\gamma_i$ at zero external momenta of
$\gamma_i$ (degree $0$) and $T^{(2)}_\Gamma$ the Taylor polynomial of degree two in $p$. By the symmetry among the three lines the three terms
$T_{\gamma_i}I_\Gamma$ are equal, each a product of a zero-momentum bubble and a one-loop tadpole. The independent integrals are
$I_\Gamma(p)$, the product $B(0)T(m^2)$, and from $T_\Gamma$ the values $I(0)$ and $\partial^2I(0)$ of the subtracted integrand: four, which give a
finite function of $p^2$ vanishing with its first derivative at $p = 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The second integrative exercise shows that the sum of all bamboo graphs is grouplike, which links the Hopf algebra to
the renormalisation group. It uses @exr-ren-hopf-toy.

::: {#exr-ren-x-grouplike}
#### The bamboo series is grouplike

For $X = \sum_{n \geq 0}\alpha^nb_n$, show that $\Delta(X) = X \otimes X$. With the toy-model values of @exr-ren-hopf-toy, compute $G(L) = \sum_n\alpha^nF_R[b_n](L)$ to
order $\alpha^4$ with Sage, and verify that $G = e^{L\gamma(\alpha)}$ with $\gamma(\alpha) = -\alpha - \frac{\pi^2}{6}\alpha^3 + O(\alpha^5)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\Delta(X) = \sum_n\alpha^n\sum_kb_k \otimes b_{n - k} = \sum_{k, l}\alpha^kb_k \otimes \alpha^lb_l = X \otimes X$. Renormalised Feynman rules are a character, and for a grouplike
element the convolution structure of @balduf2024dyson [Lemma 39] gives $F_R[X](L_1 + L_2) = F_R[X](L_1)F_R[X](L_2)$, so $F_R[X](L)$
is an exponential $e^{L\gamma}$ [@balduf2024dyson, Thm. 46]. From the four renormalised bamboos, the coefficient of $L$ is $-\alpha -
\frac{\pi^2}{6}\alpha^3$ and that of $L^2$ is $\frac{\alpha^2}{2} + \frac{\pi^2}{6}\alpha^4 = \frac{\gamma^2}{2}$, as the exponential requires; $\gamma(\alpha) = -\frac1\pi\arcsin(\pi\alpha)$ is the
exact anomalous dimension of this model (@prp-ren-linear-dse):

{{< sage exr-ren-x-grouplike >}}
:::

**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

The third integrative exercise compares the three languages of this part on one graph. It combines @exm-ren-forest-chain,
@exm-ren-hopf-chain and @exr-ren-bphz-bogoliubov.

::: {#exr-ren-x-three-languages}
#### Forests, recursion and antipode

For the chain of three bubbles in one channel, write the counterterm in the Hopf algebra, using $\Delta(\Gamma_3) = \Gamma_3 \otimes 1 + 1 \otimes \Gamma_3 +
3\,b \otimes \Gamma_2 + 2\,\Gamma_2 \otimes b + (b \cdot b) \otimes b$ where $\Gamma_2$ is the chain of two and $b \cdot b$ the outer two bubbles, and check that the number of
forests found in @exr-ren-forest-count is reproduced.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Contracting any one of the three bubbles leaves a chain of two ($3\,b \otimes \Gamma_2$); contracting either chain of two adjacent bubbles
leaves one bubble ($2\,\Gamma_2 \otimes b$); the outer two bubbles are vertex-disjoint, and contracting both leaves one bubble ($b\cdot b \otimes b$).
The counterterm is $S_R(\Gamma_3) = -R[F(\Gamma_3) + 3S_R(b)F(\Gamma_2) + 2S_R(\Gamma_2)F(b) + S_R(b)^2F(b)]$. Expanding $S_R(\Gamma_2)$ recursively, the terms
correspond to the forests of $\Gamma_3$ that do not contain $\Gamma_3$: $\emptyset$, the three single bubbles, the two pairs, the pair of outer
bubbles $\{b_1, b_3\}$, and the four forests $\{b_i, \Gamma_2\}$ with $b_i$ inside one of the chains of two: $1 + 3 + 2 + 1 + 4 = 11$, and with
$\Gamma_3$ added to each, $22$, the number found by enumeration.
:::

## Ward identities and QED at one loop {#sec-qed-one-loop}

In a gauge theory the counterterms are not independent. Gauge invariance relates the Green functions with photon
legs to those without, and these relations, the Ward identities, survive renormalisation if the regulator respects
the symmetry. In quantum electrodynamics they make the photon massless to all orders and make the renormalisation of
the charge depend only on the photon self-energy, so that every particle's charge is renormalised by the same factor.
This part states the identities and renormalises quantum electrodynamics at one loop, following @grozin2005lectures
[Sec. 3] with $d = 4 - \epsilon$ in place of his $d = 4 - 2\epsilon$, so that his $\frac1\epsilon$ is our $\frac2\epsilon$.

For more on this topic, see @gelis2021problems.

### Ward identities

The Lagrangian of quantum electrodynamics is $\bar\psi_0(i{D}\!\!\!/ - m_0)\psi_0 - \frac14F_{0\mu\nu}F_0^{\mu\nu} - \frac{1}{2a_0}(\partial_\mu A_0^\mu)^2$ with $D_\mu = \partial_\mu + ie_0A_{0\mu}$
(the sign of the charge is a convention; @grozin2005lectures writes $-ie_0$) and a gauge-fixing parameter $a_0$. Its
renormalised fields and parameters are $\psi_0 = Z_\psi^{1/2}\psi$, $A_0 = Z_A^{1/2}A$, $a_0 = Z_Aa$, $m_0 = Z_mm$ and $e_0 = Z_\alpha^{1/2}\mu^{\epsilon/2}e$
[@grozin2005lectures, eq. 3.7]. The theorem below is the statement that gauge invariance survives quantisation.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#thm-ren-ward-takahashi}
#### The Ward-Takahashi identities

In quantum electrodynamics with dimensional regularisation, to every order of perturbation theory: the photon
self-energy is transverse, $q_\mu\Pi^{\mu\nu}(q) = 0$, so $\Pi^{\mu\nu}(q) = (q^2\eta^{\mu\nu} - q^\mu q^\nu)\Pi(q^2)$; the electron-photon vertex $\Gamma^\mu(p', p)$,
normalised to $\gamma^\mu$ at tree level, satisfies
$$
q_\mu\Gamma^\mu(p', p) = S^{-1}(p') - S^{-1}(p), \qquad q = p' - p ,
$$ {#eq-ren-ward-takahashi}
where $S^{-1}(p) = {p}\!\!\!/ - m - \Sigma(p)$ is the inverse full propagator without the factor $i$; in particular $\Gamma^\mu(p, p) = \partial S^{-1}/\partial p_\mu$.
Consequently the renormalisation constants of the vertex and of the electron field satisfy $Z_\Gamma Z_\psi = 1$, and the
charge is renormalised by the photon field alone, $Z_\alpha = Z_A^{-1}$ [@grozin2005lectures, Secs. 3.3 and 3.7, eqs. 3.73-3.77].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
*Proof (outline).* At tree level, ${q}\!\!\!/ = ({p}\!\!\!/' - m) - ({p}\!\!\!/ - m)$, which multiplied by the propagators reads $S_0(p'){q}\!\!\!/S_0(p) =
S_0(p) - S_0(p')$ [@grozin2005lectures, eq. 3.18]. Contracting an external photon of any diagram with its momentum and using
this identity at the vertex where it attaches, the diagrams cancel in pairs, leaving the difference of two diagrams that
differ only by a shift of a loop momentum; in dimensional regularisation such shifts are allowed and the difference
vanishes, which gives transversality, and for the vertex the surviving terms are the two self-energies, which gives
@eq-ren-ward-takahashi. Written with renormalised quantities, $Z_\Gamma q_\mu\Gamma_r^\mu = Z_\psi^{-1}(S_r^{-1}(p') - S_r^{-1}(p))$, so $Z_\Gamma Z_\psi$ is finite;
in minimal subtraction the only finite renormalisation constant is $1$. Finally the amputated vertex with its field
normalisations, $e_0\Gamma^\mu Z_\psi Z_A^{1/2} = e_0Z_\Gamma Z_\psi Z_A^{1/2}\Gamma_r^\mu$, must be finite when expressed through $e$; with $Z_\Gamma Z_\psi = 1$ this says that
$e_0Z_A^{1/2}$ is $e\mu^{\epsilon/2}$ times a finite factor, so $Z_\alpha Z_A = 1$ in minimal subtraction. $\square$

The identity can be checked at tree level with explicit matrices, which is the induction start of the proof. The first
example does it.

::: {#exm-ren-ward-tree}
#### The identity at tree level

With $S_0^{-1}(p) = {p}\!\!\!/ - m$ and $\Gamma^\mu = \gamma^\mu$, @eq-ren-ward-takahashi reads ${q}\!\!\!/ = {p}\!\!\!/' - {p}\!\!\!/$, true for all momenta. Multiplying by $S_0(p')$ on the
left and $S_0(p)$ on the right gives $S_0(p'){q}\!\!\!/S_0(p) = S_0(p) - S_0(p')$: inserting a photon of momentum $q$, contracted with $q$, into
an electron line is the same as the difference of the line with and without the momentum shift (@exr-ren-ward-tree).
This is the graphical identity behind the cancellations of the proof.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The transversality of the photon self-energy is the reason the photon stays massless. The second example shows the
mechanism at one loop.

::: {#exm-ren-ward-transverse}
#### The photon stays massless

At one loop, $q_\mu\Pi^{\mu\nu}(q)$ is the trace of the electron loop with ${q}\!\!\!/$ inserted at one vertex, and by the tree identity it is
$\propto\int d^d\ell\,\operatorname{tr}[\gamma^\nu(S_0(\ell) - S_0(\ell + q))]$, the difference of two integrals related by the shift $\ell \to \ell + q$
[@grozin2005lectures, eq. 3.20]. In dimensional regularisation it vanishes, and $\Pi^{\mu\nu} = (q^2\eta^{\mu\nu} - q^\mu q^\nu)\Pi(q^2)$ is zero at $q = 0$: no
photon mass is generated. With a sharp cutoff the shift produces a surface term like that of @exr-ren-shift-cutoff,
and a term $\Lambda^2\eta^{\mu\nu}$ appears (@exr-rn-gauge-cutoff).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The constants $Z_\psi$ and $Z_\Gamma$ depend on the gauge, but their product does not. The third example gives both at one loop.

::: {#exm-ren-ward-z1z2}
#### The vertex and the field at one loop

In a general covariant gauge, $Z_\psi = 1 - \frac{a\alpha}{2\pi\epsilon}$ and $Z_\Gamma = 1 + \frac{a\alpha}{2\pi\epsilon}$ in minimal subtraction, so $Z_\Gamma Z_\psi = 1 + O(\alpha^2)$, as the
theorem requires [@grozin2005lectures, eqs. 3.64 and 3.84]. In the Landau gauge $a = 0$ both are $1$ at one loop; in the
Feynman gauge $a = 1$. The photon field constant $Z_A = 1 - \frac{2\alpha}{3\pi\epsilon}$ does not depend on $a$, and neither does $Z_\alpha = Z_A^{-1} =
1 + \frac{2\alpha}{3\pi\epsilon}$, which is what makes the running charge gauge independent.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Since $Z_\alpha = Z_A^{-1}$ involves only the photon, the renormalisation of a charge does not depend on which particle
carries it. The fourth example draws the consequence.

::: {#exm-ren-ward-universality}
#### Charge universality

Add a muon with charge $Q_\mu e$. Its vertex and field constants satisfy the same identity, so its bare and renormalised
charges are related by the same $Z_A^{-1/2}$: $Q_\mu e_0 = Z_A^{-1/2}Q_\mu e\mu^{\epsilon/2}$. The ratio of two charges is not renormalised, and the
equality of the proton and electron charges, measured to one part in $10^{21}$, is not spoiled by the strong
interactions of the proton. The vacuum polarisation, by contrast, receives a contribution from every charged particle
in proportion to $Q^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The exercises check the identity numerically, derive the running charge from $Z_\alpha$, and extend the identity to scalar
electrodynamics. The first uses Sage with the gamma matrices of @exm-gamma-weyl.

::: {#exr-ren-ward-tree}
#### The tree identity with matrices

With the Weyl gamma matrices, check with Sage that $({p}\!\!\!/' - m)^{-1}{q}\!\!\!/({p}\!\!\!/ - m)^{-1} = ({p}\!\!\!/ - m)^{-1} - ({p}\!\!\!/' - m)^{-1}$ for random numerical
momenta $p$, $p'$ and $q = p' - p$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Multiplying the claimed identity by $({p}\!\!\!/' - m)$ on the left and $({p}\!\!\!/ - m)$ on the right gives ${q}\!\!\!/ = ({p}\!\!\!/' - m) - ({p}\!\!\!/ - m)$, which is
linear algebra; numerically the difference of the two sides vanishes to rounding error:

{{< sage exr-ren-ward-tree >}}
:::

The running of the charge follows from $Z_\alpha$ by the method of @exr-ren-ct-multiplicative. The second exercise derives it
and its generalisation to several fermions.

::: {#exr-ren-ward-beta}
#### The beta function of quantum electrodynamics

From $\alpha_0\mu^{-\epsilon} = Z_\alpha\alpha$ with $Z_\alpha = 1 + \frac{2\alpha}{3\pi\epsilon}\sum_fQ_f^2$, derive $\mu\frac{d\alpha}{d\mu} = -\epsilon\alpha + \frac{2\alpha^2}{3\pi}\sum_fQ_f^2$, and the beta function of $e$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Differentiating at fixed $\alpha_0$: $-\epsilon Z_\alpha\alpha = \beta_\alpha(Z_\alpha + \alpha Z_\alpha')$. With $\beta_\alpha = -\epsilon\alpha + b\alpha^2$ and $Z_\alpha = 1 + \frac{c\alpha}{\epsilon}$, $c = \frac{2}{3\pi}\sum Q_f^2$,
the order $\alpha^2$ terms give $-c\alpha^2 = b\alpha^2 - 2c\alpha^2$, so $b = c$. Since $\alpha = e^2/4\pi$, $\mu\frac{de}{d\mu} = \frac{e}{2\alpha}\mu\frac{d\alpha}{d\mu} = \frac{e^3}{12\pi^2}\sum_fQ_f^2$
at $\epsilon = 0$, the value quoted in @exm-rn-qed, now derived.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Scalar electrodynamics has a second interaction, the seagull $e^2A_\mu A^\mu\phi^*\phi$, which the Ward identity needs. The third
exercise shows why.

::: {#exr-ren-ward-scalar}
#### Scalar electrodynamics

For a charged scalar the one-loop photon self-energy has a bubble, $\propto\int d^d\ell\frac{(2\ell + q)^\mu(2\ell + q)^\nu}{(\ell^2 - m^2)((\ell + q)^2 - m^2)}$, and a seagull,
$\propto -2\eta^{\mu\nu}\int d^d\ell\frac{1}{\ell^2 - m^2}$. Show that $q_\mu$ times the bubble is a difference of two tadpoles, and that the seagull with its
coefficient cancels it, so that only the sum is transverse.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$q\cdot(2\ell + q) = ((\ell + q)^2 - m^2) - (\ell^2 - m^2)$, so $q_\mu$ times the bubble integrand is $(2\ell + q)^\nu(\frac{1}{\ell^2 - m^2} - \frac{1}{(\ell + q)^2 - m^2})$.
The first term integrates to $q^\nu\int\frac{1}{\ell^2 - m^2}$ (the $2\ell^\nu$ part vanishes by symmetry); in the second, shift $\ell \to \ell - q$: $(2\ell - q)^\nu\frac{1}{\ell^2 - m^2}$
integrates to $-q^\nu\int\frac{1}{\ell^2 - m^2}$. The difference is $2q^\nu\int\frac{1}{\ell^2 - m^2}$, which is exactly cancelled by $q_\mu$ times the seagull
$-2\eta^{\mu\nu}\int\frac{1}{\ell^2 - m^2}$. Without the seagull, demanded by gauge invariance of $|D_\mu\phi|^2$, the photon would acquire a mass.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The longitudinal part of the photon propagator is not renormalised at all, a second consequence of transversality.
The fourth exercise derives it [@grozin2005lectures, Sec. 3.2].

::: {#exr-ren-ward-longitudinal}
#### The longitudinal photon

Using $\Pi^{\mu\nu} = (q^2\eta^{\mu\nu} - q^\mu q^\nu)\Pi$ and the Dyson series, show that the full photon propagator is $\frac{-i}{q^2(1 - \Pi(q^2))}(\eta_{\mu\nu} -
\frac{q_\mu q_\nu}{q^2}) - ia_0\frac{q_\mu q_\nu}{(q^2)^2}$, and explain why $a_0$ and $A_0$ are renormalised by the same $Z_A$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The free propagator is $-i(\eta_{\mu\nu} - (1 - a_0)\frac{q_\mu q_\nu}{q^2})/q^2$. The self-energy is proportional to the transverse projector $P_{\mu\nu} = \eta_{\mu\nu} -
q_\mu q_\nu/q^2$, which annihilates the longitudinal projector $L_{\mu\nu} = q_\mu q_\nu/q^2$; in the geometric series only the transverse part
is dressed, $\frac{P}{q^2}(1 + \Pi + \Pi^2 + \dots)$, and the longitudinal part $a_0L/q^2$ is untouched. The renormalised propagator is the bare
one divided by $Z_A$, so the longitudinal part is finite only if $a_0/Z_A = a$ is: the gauge parameter renormalises
like the field.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

### QED at one loop

The photon self-energy decides how the strength of the electromagnetic interaction depends on the distance. At large
distances the vacuum is polarised by virtual pairs and screens a charge; at distances shorter than the Compton
wavelength of the electron the screening is partly undone, and the effective charge grows. The figure shows both
effects.

![The vacuum polarisation of one electron loop. Left: the Uehling correction to the Coulomb potential,
$V(r)/V_{\mathrm{Coulomb}} - 1$, in units of $\alpha$, against $m_er$: the charge seen at distance $r$ grows as $r$ falls below the
Compton wavelength $1/m_e$. Right: the renormalised vacuum polarisation $\hat\Pi(s)$ for time-like $s$, in units of $\alpha$:
real part (solid) and imaginary part (dashed), which starts at the pair threshold $s = 4m_e^2$ and tends to $\frac\alpha3$, the
total cross section of pair production. Generated by `figures/ren-vacuum-polarisation.sage`.](figures/ren-vacuum-polarisation.svg){#fig-ren-vacuum-polarisation width=95%}

The definition fixes the normalisation of the vacuum polarisation and the effective coupling it defines. The
subtraction at $q^2 = 0$ is the on-shell scheme of @def-ren-scheme.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-ren-vacuum-polarisation}
#### Vacuum polarisation

The **vacuum polarisation** is the one-particle-irreducible photon self-energy $i\Pi^{\mu\nu}(q) = i(q^2\eta^{\mu\nu} - q^\mu q^\nu)\Pi(q^2)$, so that the
transverse part of the full photon propagator is $\frac{-i}{q^2(1 - \Pi(q^2))}$. With $\hat\Pi(q^2) = \Pi(q^2) - \Pi(0)$ and the on-shell charge $\alpha$,
the **effective coupling** at momentum $q$ is
$$
\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}(q^2) = \frac{\alpha}{1 - \hat\Pi(q^2)} ,
$$ {#eq-ren-alpha-eff}
the strength with which two charges exchanging a photon of momentum $q$ interact.
:::

:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The one-loop vacuum polarisation is a single Feynman-parameter integral. The first example gives it in the two schemes
of interest.

::: {#exm-ren-vp-one-loop}
#### The electron loop

Computing the trace and the integral in $d$ dimensions [@grozin2005lectures, eqs. 3.22-3.35, with a mass],
$$
\Pi(q^2) = -\frac{2\alpha}{\pi}\int_0^1dx\,x(1 - x)\Bigl(\frac2{\bar\epsilon} - \log\frac{m^2 - x(1 - x)q^2}{\mu^2}\Bigr), \qquad
\hat\Pi(q^2) = -\frac{2\alpha}{\pi}\int_0^1dx\,x(1 - x)\log\frac{m^2}{m^2 - x(1 - x)q^2} .
$$
The pole $-\frac{2\alpha}{\pi}\cdot\frac16\cdot\frac{2}{\bar\epsilon} = -\frac{2\alpha}{3\pi\bar\epsilon}$ is removed by $Z_A$ (@exm-ren-ward-z1z2); for space-like $q^2 = -Q^2 < 0$, $\hat\Pi > 0$
and the effective coupling grows with $Q$ (@exr-ren-vp-limits).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

At small momentum transfer the vacuum polarisation adds a contact term to the Coulomb potential. The second example
evaluates it for hydrogen, where it is part of the Lamb shift that the Dirac equation misses (@sec-dirac-hydrogen).

::: {#exm-ren-vp-uehling}
#### The Uehling term and the Lamb shift

For $|q^2| \ll m^2$, $\hat\Pi(q^2) = -\frac{\alpha}{15\pi}\frac{q^2}{m^2} + O(q^4)$. For a static potential $q^2 = -\vec q^{\,2}$, and $-\frac{4\pi\alpha}{\vec q^{\,2}}(1 +
\hat\Pi) = -\frac{4\pi\alpha}{\vec q^{\,2}} - \frac{4\alpha^2}{15m^2}$, so $V(\vec r) = -\frac\alpha r - \frac{4\alpha^2}{15m^2}\delta^3(\vec r)$. In first-order perturbation theory, with
$|\psi_{n00}(0)|^2 = \frac{(m\alpha)^3}{\pi n^3}$, the $nS$ levels of hydrogen shift by $\Delta E = -\frac{4\alpha^5m}{15\pi n^3}$, which for $2S$ is $-1.12 \times 10^{-7}\,\mathrm{eV}$ or
$-27.1\,\mathrm{MHz}$ (@exr-ren-vp-lamb), about $-2.6\%$ of the measured Lamb shift of $1057.8\,\mathrm{MHz}$, whose bulk comes from the
electron self-energy.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

At large space-like momentum the logarithm dominates. The third example gives the effective coupling there and
compares it with the running coupling of the minimal scheme.

::: {#exm-ren-vp-large}
#### The effective coupling at large momentum

For $Q^2 = -q^2 \gg m^2$, $\hat\Pi = \frac{\alpha}{3\pi}(\log\frac{Q^2}{m^2} - \frac53) + O(m^2/Q^2)$, so
$$
\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}(Q) = \frac{\alpha}{1 - \frac{\alpha}{3\pi}\bigl(\log\frac{Q^2}{m^2} - \frac53\bigr)} .
$$
Its inverse falls by $\frac{2}{3\pi}$ per unit of $\log Q$, the rate of the $\overline{\mathrm{MS}}$ coupling (@exm-ren-sch-on-shell-qed), and the constant $\frac53$
is the scheme difference of @exr-ren-x-qed-schemes. The geometric series in @eq-ren-alpha-eff resums the leading
logarithms $(\alpha\log Q^2)^n$ of all orders, the Gell-Mann-Low result of @balduf2024dyson [Example 106].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Above the threshold for pair production the vacuum polarisation has an imaginary part. The fourth example relates it to
a cross section.

::: {#exm-ren-vp-imaginary}
#### The imaginary part and pair production

For time-like $s = q^2 > 4m^2$ the logarithm has a cut, and with $\beta = \sqrt{1 - 4m^2/s}$, $|\operatorname{Im}\hat\Pi(s)| = \frac\alpha3\beta\frac{3 - \beta^2}{2}$
(@exr-ren-vp-imaginary). By unitarity this is proportional to the total rate of $\gamma^* \to e^+e^-$, and the cross section of
$e^+e^- \to \mu^+\mu^-$ near the muon threshold is $\sigma = \frac{4\pi\alpha^2}{3s}\beta_\mu\frac{3 - \beta_\mu^2}{2}$, which tends to $\frac{4\pi\alpha^2}{3s} = \frac{86.8\,\mathrm{nb}}{s/\mathrm{GeV}^2}$ at high
energy. The ratio of the hadronic rate to this one counts the colours and charges of the quarks.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The exercises expand the vacuum polarisation, compute the Uehling shift, and derive the imaginary part. The first is a
Sage expansion of the integral of @exm-ren-vp-one-loop.

::: {#exr-ren-vp-limits}
#### Two limits of the vacuum polarisation

Expand $\hat\Pi(-Q^2)$ for $Q \ll m$ to order $Q^4$ and for $Q \gg m$ to order $Q^0$ with Sage, and confirm @exm-ren-vp-uehling and @exm-ren-vp-large.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $z = Q^2/m^2$, $\hat\Pi = \frac{2\alpha}{\pi}\int_0^1x(1 - x)\log(1 + x(1 - x)z)dx = \frac{2\alpha}{\pi}(\frac{z}{30} - \frac{z^2}{280} + \dots)$ for small $z$, which is $-\frac{\alpha}{15\pi}\frac{q^2}{m^2} + O(q^4)$ with $q^2 = -Q^2$, and
$\frac{\alpha}{3\pi}(\log z - \frac53) + O(\log z/z)$ for large $z$:

{{< sage exr-ren-vp-limits >}}
:::

**Lean.** Pending.

The Uehling contribution to the hydrogen Lamb shift is a number that can be compared with experiment. The second
exercise computes it.

::: {#exr-ren-vp-lamb}
#### The Uehling shift of hydrogen

Evaluate $\Delta E = -\frac{4\alpha^5m_e}{15\pi n^3}$ for $n = 1, 2$ in eV and in MHz, and compare the $2S$ value with the measured $2S_{1/2} - 2P_{1/2}$
splitting of $1057.8\,\mathrm{MHz}$. Why does the $2P$ level not shift at this order?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $\alpha = 1/137.036$ and $m_e = 510\,999\,\mathrm{eV}$, $\frac{4\alpha^5m_e}{15\pi} = 8.98 \times 10^{-7}\,\mathrm{eV}$; for $n = 1$ the shift is $-8.98 \times 10^{-7}\,\mathrm{eV} = -217\,\mathrm{MHz}$,
for $n = 2$ it is $-1.12 \times 10^{-7}\,\mathrm{eV} = -27.1\,\mathrm{MHz}$. The $P$ states vanish at the origin, so the contact term does not
shift them. The Uehling term lowers $2S$ by $27\,\mathrm{MHz}$, while the full Lamb shift raises it by $1058\,\mathrm{MHz}$:

{{< sage exr-ren-vp-lamb >}}
:::

**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

The imaginary part of the vacuum polarisation comes from the region where the argument of the logarithm is negative.
The third exercise computes it.

::: {#exr-ren-vp-imaginary}
#### The imaginary part

For $s > 4m^2$, find the interval of $x$ where $m^2 - x(1 - x)s < 0$, and show that $|\operatorname{Im}\hat\Pi(s + i0)| = 2\alpha\int x(1 - x)dx$ over that interval
equals $\frac\alpha3\beta\frac{3 - \beta^2}{2}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The roots of $x(1 - x)s = m^2$ are $x_\pm = \frac{1 \pm \beta}{2}$, and on $(x_-, x_+)$ the logarithm has imaginary part $\mp\pi$; the prefactor $\frac{2\alpha}{\pi}$ turns
it into $2\alpha\int_{x_-}^{x_+}x(1 - x)dx$. With $x = \frac{1 + t}{2}$, $x(1 - x) = \frac{1 - t^2}{4}$ and $dx = \frac{dt}{2}$, so the integral is $\frac18\int_{-\beta}^\beta(1 - t^2)dt = \frac{\beta}{4} -
\frac{\beta^3}{12} = \frac{\beta(3 - \beta^2)}{12}$, and $2\alpha$ times it is $\frac{\alpha}{3}\beta\frac{3 - \beta^2}{2}$. As $\beta \to 1$ it tends to $\frac\alpha3$, the limit in
@fig-ren-vacuum-polarisation.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

With the vacuum polarisation in hand, the self-energy and the vertex of the electron complete the one-loop picture.
The proposition collects the resulting constants, the running and the magnetic moment.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-ren-qed-one-loop}
#### Quantum electrodynamics at one loop

In the modified minimal scheme with $d = 4 - \epsilon$ and a covariant gauge with parameter $a$, the one-loop renormalisation
constants of quantum electrodynamics with one electron are
$$
Z_A = 1 - \frac{2\alpha}{3\pi\bar\epsilon}, \quad Z_\alpha = 1 + \frac{2\alpha}{3\pi\bar\epsilon}, \quad Z_\psi = 1 - \frac{a\alpha}{2\pi\bar\epsilon}, \quad Z_m = 1 - \frac{3\alpha}{2\pi\bar\epsilon},
$$
the running coupling and mass obey $\mu\frac{d\alpha}{d\mu} = \frac{2\alpha^2}{3\pi}$ and $\mu\frac{dm}{d\mu} = -\frac{3\alpha}{2\pi}m$, and the magnetic form factor of the
electron at zero momentum transfer is $F_2(0) = \frac{\alpha}{2\pi}$, the anomalous magnetic moment $\frac{g - 2}{2}$ at order $\alpha$
[@grozin2005lectures, eqs. 3.42, 3.64, 3.88, 3.104-3.107 and Sec. 6.5].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
*Proof.* These are Grozin's results with $\frac1\epsilon \to \frac2\epsilon$. $Z_A$ follows from @exm-ren-vp-one-loop, $Z_\alpha$ from the theorem, $Z_\psi$ from
the one-loop self-energy $\Sigma_V$, which vanishes in the Landau gauge, and $Z_m$ from the scalar part of the self-energy,
which is gauge independent. The running follows from $\alpha_0\mu^{-\epsilon} = Z_\alpha\alpha$ (@exr-ren-ward-beta) and from $m_0 = Z_mm$, as in
@prp-ren-phi4-one-loop. The form factor $F_2$ is ultraviolet finite and needs no counterterm; its value is computed in the
reference from the vertex on the mass shell. $\square$

The beta function of the proposition is that of one charged fermion. The first example adds the other charged
particles of the Standard Model below the $Z$ mass.

::: {#exm-ren-qed-flavours}
#### Many charged fermions

Each Dirac fermion of charge $Q_f$ and $N_c$ colours adds $N_cQ_f^2$ to $\sum Q^2$, so $\mu\frac{d\alpha}{d\mu} = \frac{2\alpha^2}{3\pi}\sum_fN_cQ_f^2$ above all their
masses. Below the $Z$ mass and above the $b$ quark: three leptons ($3$), the $u$ and $c$ quarks ($2 \times 3 \times \frac49 = \frac83$) and the $d$,
$s$, $b$ quarks ($3 \times 3 \times \frac19 = 1$), a total of $\frac{20}{3}$, so the running is about seven times faster than with the electron alone.
The light quarks below $1\,\mathrm{GeV}$ are not free particles, and their contribution is taken from the measured $e^+e^-$
cross section through the imaginary part of @exm-ren-vp-imaginary.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The electron mass runs downwards as the scale grows, unlike the charge, which runs upwards. The second example
estimates how much it changes between the electron mass and the $Z$ mass.

::: {#exm-ren-qed-mass}
#### The running electron mass

With $\mu\frac{dm}{d\mu} = -\frac{3\alpha}{2\pi}m$ and $\alpha$ nearly constant, $m(\mu) = m(\mu_0)(\mu/\mu_0)^{-3\alpha/2\pi}$. From $m_e$ to $M_Z$, $\log\frac{M_Z}{m_e} = 12.1$ and the
mass falls by the factor $e^{-0.042} = 0.959$, about $4\%$. The pole mass, by contrast, is a fixed physical number; the running
mass is the parameter that enters high-energy processes without large logarithms (@exr-ren-sch-pole-mass).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The anomalous magnetic moment is the most precisely tested prediction of quantum field theory. The third example
compares the one-loop value with the measurement.

::: {#exm-ren-qed-g2}
#### The anomalous magnetic moment

With $\alpha = 1/137.036$, $\frac{\alpha}{2\pi} = 0.001\,161\,41$, against the measured $\frac{g}{2} - 1 = 0.001\,159\,652\,18$ [@fan2023electron, eq. 6]. The
one-loop term accounts for the measured value to $0.15\%$, and the rest is a series $C_4(\frac\alpha\pi)^2 + C_6(\frac\alpha\pi)^3 + \dots$ with
coefficients computed to the fifth order [@fan2023electron, eq. 7]; the coefficient $C_4 \approx -0.33$ can be read off from the
difference (@exr-ren-qed-g2). The quantity $F_2(0)$ needs no renormalisation of its own, because no counterterm of
dimension at most four has its spin structure $\sigma^{\mu\nu}q_\nu$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The exercises derive the mass counterterm from the self-energy, discuss gauge dependence, and extract the two-loop
coefficient of the magnetic moment from data. The first derivation follows @grozin2005lectures [Sec. 3.8].

::: {#exr-ren-qed-mass-ct}
#### The mass counterterm

The one-loop electron self-energy in the Feynman gauge has the pole part $\Sigma(p) = \frac{\alpha}{4\pi}\frac{2}{\epsilon}(-{p}\!\!\!/ + 4m) + \text{finite}$. Show that the
pole mass $m_P = m_0 + \Sigma({p}\!\!\!/ = m)$ is finite with $m_0 = Z_mm$, $Z_m = 1 - \frac{3\alpha}{2\pi\epsilon}$, and that $Z_\psi = 1 - \frac{\alpha}{2\pi\epsilon}$ follows from the ${p}\!\!\!/$ term.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
On the mass shell the pole part is $\frac{\alpha}{4\pi}\frac2\epsilon(-m + 4m) = \frac{3\alpha m}{2\pi\epsilon}$, so $m_P = m_0 + \frac{3\alpha m}{2\pi\epsilon} + \text{finite}$, and $m_0 = m(1 - \frac{3\alpha}{2\pi\epsilon})$
cancels the pole. The ${p}\!\!\!/$ term rescales the residue: $S^{-1} = {p}\!\!\!/(1 + \frac{\alpha}{2\pi\epsilon}) - \dots$, so with $\psi_0 = Z_\psi^{1/2}\psi$ the renormalised
inverse propagator $Z_\psi S^{-1}$ is finite for $Z_\psi = 1 - \frac{\alpha}{2\pi\epsilon}$, the value of the proposition at $a = 1$. (With the field
rescaled, $m_0 = Z_m m$ is the relation for the mass, and the combination $Z_\psi Z_m$ multiplies $m$ in the Lagrangian.)
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The field constant depends on the gauge, but nothing physical does, and the two statements must be reconciled. The
second exercise explains why they are consistent.

::: {#exr-ren-qed-gauge}
#### Gauge dependence

Explain why $Z_\psi$ may depend on $a$ while $Z_m$, $Z_\alpha$ and the pole mass may not, and give the value of $a$ for which the
electron field is not renormalised at one loop.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The electron field is not gauge invariant, $\psi \to e^{-ie\theta}\psi$, and its correlation functions depend on the gauge, so their
normalisation may as well. The pole mass is the position of a pole of a physical amplitude, the charge is fixed by a
physical scattering amplitude, and $Z_m$, $Z_\alpha$ in a mass-independent scheme are determined by them. In the Landau gauge $a = 0$,
$Z_\psi = 1$ at one loop [@grozin2005lectures, eq. 3.61].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The two-loop coefficient of the magnetic moment can be estimated from the measurement. The third exercise does it with
Sage.

::: {#exr-ren-qed-g2}
#### The second coefficient from data

Assuming $\frac g2 - 1 = \frac12\frac\alpha\pi + C_4(\frac\alpha\pi)^2$ with the higher orders neglected, solve for $C_4$ with the measured value
$0.001\,159\,652\,180\,59$ and $\alpha = 1/137.035\,999$. How large is the neglected third-order term if $|C_6| \approx 1.2$?

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\frac\alpha\pi = 0.002\,322\,819$, $\frac12\frac\alpha\pi = 0.001\,161\,410$, and the difference $-1.758 \times 10^{-6}$ divided by $(\alpha/\pi)^2 = 5.396 \times 10^{-6}$ gives
$C_4 \approx -0.3257$. A third-order term $1.2(\alpha/\pi)^3 = 1.5 \times 10^{-8}$ shifts this estimate by $1.5 \times 10^{-8}/5.4 \times 10^{-6} \approx 0.003$, so the
estimate is close to the exact coefficient, which is known in closed form:

{{< sage exr-ren-qed-g2 >}}

### Exercises

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first integrative exercise computes the effective electromagnetic coupling at the $Z$ mass from the charged leptons
alone, with the exact one-loop vacuum polarisation. It combines @def-ren-vacuum-polarisation with
@exm-ren-qed-flavours.

::: {#exr-ren-x-alpha-leptons}
#### Leptons and the coupling at the $Z$ mass

Compute $1/\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}(M_Z)$ with the electron, muon and tau loops, using the exact one-loop $\hat\Pi$ for each, and compare with the
leading-logarithm formula. How much do the quarks have to contribute to reach the measured $128.9$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Each lepton contributes $\frac{2}{\pi}\int_0^1x(1 - x)\log(1 + x(1 - x)M_Z^2/m_\ell^2)dx$ to $1 - \hat\Pi$ divided by $\alpha$; the three together reduce
$137.036$ to $132.73$, and the leading logarithms with the constant $\frac53$ give the same to three decimals, the masses being
all far below $M_Z$. The quarks must supply the remaining $\Delta(1/\alpha) \approx 3.8$:

{{< sage exr-ren-x-alpha-leptons >}}
:::

The second integrative exercise shows that the Ward identity holds in the on-shell scheme as well. It combines
@thm-ren-ward-takahashi with @def-ren-scheme.

::: {#exr-ren-x-ward-on-shell}
#### The Ward identity on the mass shell

In the on-shell scheme the electron residue constant $Z_\psi^{\mathrm{os}}$ makes the propagator $\frac{1}{{p}\!\!\!/ - m}$ near the pole, and the charge is
defined by the vertex at $q = 0$. Use $\Gamma^\mu(p, p) = \partial S^{-1}/\partial p_\mu$ to show $Z_\psi^{\mathrm{os}}Z_\Gamma^{\mathrm{os}} = 1$ and $Z_\alpha^{\mathrm{os}} = (Z_A^{\mathrm{os}})^{-1}$
[@grozin2005lectures, eqs. 6.37-6.38].
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Near the mass shell $S(p) = \frac{Z_\psi^{\mathrm{os}}}{{p}\!\!\!/ - m}$, so $S^{-1} = (Z_\psi^{\mathrm{os}})^{-1}({p}\!\!\!/ - m)$ and $\Gamma^\mu(p, p) = \partial S^{-1}/\partial p_\mu = (Z_\psi^{\mathrm{os}})^{-1}\gamma^\mu$. The
on-shell vertex constant is defined by $\Gamma^\mu(p, p) = Z_\Gamma^{\mathrm{os}}\gamma^\mu$, hence $Z_\psi^{\mathrm{os}}Z_\Gamma^{\mathrm{os}} = 1$. The physical vertex is $e_0\Gamma^\mu Z_\psi^{\mathrm{os}}(Z_A^{\mathrm{os}})^{1/2}$,
and defining it to be $e\gamma^\mu$ gives $e_0(Z_A^{\mathrm{os}})^{1/2} = e$: the on-shell charge is fixed by the photon field constant alone, in every
scheme that respects gauge invariance.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The third integrative exercise evaluates the Uehling potential beyond the contact approximation. It combines the
vacuum polarisation with the Fourier transform of a Yukawa-like spectral integral.

::: {#exr-ren-x-uehling-potential}
#### The Uehling potential

The one-loop potential of a point charge is $V(r) = -\frac\alpha r\bigl(1 + \frac{2\alpha}{3\pi}\int_1^\infty du\,e^{-2mru}(1 + \frac{1}{2u^2})\frac{\sqrt{u^2 - 1}}{u^2}\bigr)$.
Evaluate the correction at $mr = 0.01, 0.1, 1$ with Sage, and show that for $mr \ll 1$ it grows like $\frac{2\alpha}{3\pi}(\log\frac{1}{mr} - \gamma_E -
\frac56)$, the logarithm of the running coupling at $Q \sim 1/r$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Each $u$ contributes a Yukawa potential of range $1/(2mu)$, weighted by the spectral function, which is the imaginary part of
@exm-ren-vp-imaginary with $s = 4m^2u^2$. Numerically the bracketed correction, in units of $\frac{2\alpha}{3\pi}$, is $3.22$, $1.11$ and
$0.036$ at $mr = 0.01, 0.1, 1$, against $3.19$ from the asymptotic formula at $mr = 0.01$. For small $mr$ the integral is dominated by $1 \ll u \ll 1/(mr)$, where the integrand is
$e^{-2mru}/u$, giving $\log\frac{1}{mr} - \gamma_E - \frac56$ up to $O(mr)$: at short distances the charge is $\alpha(1 + \frac{2\alpha}{3\pi}\log\frac{1}{mr})$, the
running coupling at $Q = 1/r$:

{{< sage exr-ren-x-uehling-potential >}}
:::

## The renormalisation group {#sec-renormalisation-group}

The bare theory knows nothing about the scale $\mu$, so a change of $\mu$ must be compensated by a change of the
renormalised parameters and of the normalisation of the fields. The transformations that do this form a group under
composition, the **renormalisation group**, and its generators are the beta functions and anomalous dimensions. The
equations they satisfy turn logarithms of fixed-order perturbation theory into running couplings, and they decide
what a theory does at very high and very low energies [@balduf2024dyson, Sec. 3.2; @grozin2005lectures, Secs. 3.5-3.7].

For more on this topic, see @buchbinder2021introduction [Ch. 13-15], @kivelson2024statistical [Ch. 10] and @shankar2017quantum [Ch. 11-14].

### The renormalisation-group equations

At fixed order, perturbation theory produces powers of $\lambda\log(Q/\mu)$, which are small only if $\mu$ is close to the
energy $Q$ of the process. The renormalisation group equation says how a Green function changes when $\mu$ changes, and
solving it replaces the fixed-order logarithms by the running coupling at the scale $Q$. The figure shows the difference
for the quartic theory.

![Renormalisation-group improvement for the massless quartic theory with $\lambda(\mu_0) = 4$. The scattering strength $-\mathcal M$ at
the symmetric point $s = t = u = -Q^2$, divided by $\lambda(\mu_0)$, against $\log(Q/\mu_0)$: at fixed order with $\mu = \mu_0$
($-\mathcal M = \lambda + b\lambda^2\log(Q/\mu_0) - b\lambda^2$, dashed), improved by setting $\mu = Q$ with the one-loop running coupling (solid), and
with the two-loop running (dotted). The fixed-order line grows linearly in the logarithm, the improved ones grow
faster and resum the leading logarithms. Generated by `figures/ren-callan-symanzik.sage`.](figures/ren-callan-symanzik.svg){#fig-ren-callan-symanzik width=70%}

The definition gives the coefficient that measures how the normalisation of a field depends on the scale. It is the
second generator of the renormalisation group, after the beta function.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-ren-anomalous-dimension}
#### Anomalous dimension

For a field renormalised by $\phi_0 = Z^{1/2}\phi$, the **anomalous dimension** is
$$
\gamma_\phi = \frac12\mu\frac{d\log Z}{d\mu}\Big|_{\text{bare fixed}} ,
$$
a function of the renormalised couplings. More generally, an operator renormalised by $\mathcal O_0 = Z_{\mathcal O}\mathcal O$ has anomalous
dimension $\gamma_{\mathcal O} = \mu\frac{d\log Z_{\mathcal O}}{d\mu}$, and a mass the anomalous dimension $\gamma_{m^2} = \mu\frac{d\log m^2}{d\mu}$. At a zero $\lambda^*$ of the beta
function the field scales with the dimension $\Delta_\phi = \frac{d - 2}{2} + \gamma_\phi(\lambda^*)$ instead of its classical dimension.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The quartic theory acquires a field anomalous dimension first at two loops. The first example recalls it and its
value at the fixed point in $d = 4 - \epsilon$.

::: {#exm-ren-ad-phi4}
#### The quartic theory

From the sunset (@exm-ren-2l-sunset), $\gamma_\phi = \frac{u^2}{12}$ with $u = \lambda/16\pi^2$, and from @prp-ren-phi4-one-loop, $\gamma_{m^2} = u$ at one loop.
At the zero $u^* = \epsilon/3$ of $\beta = -\epsilon\lambda + 3u\lambda$, $\gamma_\phi^* = \frac{\epsilon^2}{108}$: the two-point function of the critical theory falls like
$|x|^{-(d - 2 + 2\gamma_\phi^*)}$, with $2\gamma_\phi^* = \frac{\epsilon^2}{54}$ the critical exponent $\eta$ (@exr-ren-2l-anomalous).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

In a gauge theory the anomalous dimension of a charged field depends on the gauge. The second example computes it for
the electron.

::: {#exm-ren-ad-qed}
#### The electron field

With $Z_\psi = 1 - \frac{a\alpha}{2\pi\epsilon}$ (@prp-ren-qed-one-loop) and $\mu\frac{d\alpha}{d\mu} = -\epsilon\alpha + O(\alpha^2)$, $\gamma_\psi = \frac12(-\epsilon\alpha)\cdot(-\frac{a}{2\pi\epsilon}) = \frac{a\alpha}{4\pi}$, which
vanishes in the Landau gauge [@grozin2005lectures, eq. 3.68, whose $\gamma_\psi$ lacks our factor $\frac12$]. The photon has $\gamma_A = \frac12\mu\frac{d\log Z_A}{d\mu} =
\frac{\alpha}{3\pi}$, gauge independent, and $Z_\alpha = Z_A^{-1}$ gives $\mu\frac{d\log\alpha}{d\mu} = 2\gamma_A$ at $\epsilon = 0$: the running of the charge is the anomalous
dimension of the photon.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

At a fixed point the anomalous dimension is a number, and it changes the power law of correlations. The third example
shows how this appears in momentum space.

::: {#exm-ren-ad-scaling}
#### Scaling at a fixed point

If $\beta(\lambda^*) = 0$, the renormalisation group equation of the theorem below reduces for the two-point function to
$(\mu\partial_\mu + 2\gamma_\phi^*)G = 0$; with dimensional analysis, $G(p) = p^{-2}g(p/\mu)$, and since $\mu\partial_\mu g(p/\mu) = -xg'(x)$ with $x = p/\mu$,
this gives $g \propto x^{2\gamma^*}$ and $G(p) \propto p^{-2 + \eta}$ with $\eta = 2\gamma^*$ (unitarity requires $\eta \geq 0$). In position space this is $|x|^{-(d - 2 + \eta)}$
(@exr-ren-ad-fourier). This is the form in which anomalous dimensions are measured, as critical exponents of
correlation functions.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The exercises compute anomalous dimensions from renormalisation constants, count the channels of the mass anomalous
dimension in the $O(n)$ model, and relate the scaling in momentum and position space. The first is short.

::: {#exr-ren-ad-gamma-a}
#### The anomalous dimension of the photon

From $Z_A = 1 - \frac{2\alpha}{3\pi\epsilon}\sum_fQ_f^2$, compute $\gamma_A$, and check $\mu\frac{d\log\alpha}{d\mu} = 2\gamma_A$ against @exr-ren-ward-beta.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\gamma_A = \frac12\mu\frac{d\log Z_A}{d\mu} = \frac12(-\epsilon\alpha)(-\frac{2}{3\pi\epsilon}\sum Q_f^2) = \frac{\alpha}{3\pi}\sum Q_f^2$. Since $\alpha_0\mu^{-\epsilon} = \alpha Z_A^{-1}$ and $\alpha_0$ is fixed,
$\mu\frac{d\log\alpha}{d\mu} = -\epsilon + \mu\frac{d\log Z_A}{d\mu} = -\epsilon + 2\gamma_A$, so at $\epsilon = 0$, $\mu\frac{d\alpha}{d\mu} = \frac{2\alpha^2}{3\pi}\sum Q_f^2$, the result of @exr-ren-ward-beta.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

In the $O(n)$ model the mass term $\phi_a\phi_a$ and the interaction $(\phi_a\phi_a)^2$ have different tensor structures, and the
one-loop coefficients count channels. The second exercise finds the mass anomalous dimension.

::: {#exr-ren-ad-on-mass}
#### The mass anomalous dimension of the $O(n)$ model

With the interaction $\frac{\lambda}{4!}(\phi_a\phi_a)^2$, the four-point vertex is $-\frac\lambda3(\delta_{ab}\delta_{cd} + \delta_{ac}\delta_{bd} + \delta_{ad}\delta_{bc})$. Show that the tadpole contribution
to the self-energy of $\phi_a$ is $\frac{n + 2}{6}\lambda T\,\delta_{ab}$, and deduce $\gamma_{m^2} = \frac{(n + 2)}{3}\frac{\lambda}{16\pi^2}$, which is $u$ for $n = 1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Closing the lines $c$, $d$ of the vertex into a loop gives $-\frac\lambda3(\delta_{ab}n + 2\delta_{ab})$ times $\frac12T$ (the symmetry factor of the
tadpole), so $M^2 = \frac{(n + 2)\lambda}{6}T$, which for $n = 1$ is $\frac\lambda2T$ as in @prp-ren-phi4-one-loop. The pole of $T$ is $-\frac{2m^2}{16\pi^2\epsilon}$, so
$\delta_m = \frac{(n + 2)\lambda m^2}{3\cdot16\pi^2\epsilon}$ and, as in the proposition, $\gamma_{m^2} = \frac{n + 2}{3}\frac{\lambda}{16\pi^2}$, the first term of
@kompaniets2017minimally [eq. 8] (with their opposite sign convention).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A power law in momentum is a power law in position, with a related exponent. The third exercise computes the Fourier
transform with Sage.

::: {#exr-ren-ad-fourier}
#### Power laws in two spaces

Using $\int\frac{d^dp}{(2\pi)^d}\frac{e^{ip\cdot x}}{(p^2)^a} = \frac{\Gamma(d/2 - a)}{4^a\pi^{d/2}\Gamma(a)}|x|^{2a - d}$, show that $G(p) = p^{-2 + \eta}$ corresponds to $|x|^{-(d - 2 + \eta)}$, and
check the formula with Sage for $d = 3$, $a = 1$, where $G(x) = \frac{1}{4\pi|x|}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $a = 1 - \eta/2$, $|x|^{2a - d} = |x|^{2 - \eta - d}$, so the exponent is $d - 2 + \eta$. For $d = 3$, $a = 1$, $\frac{\Gamma(1/2)}{4\pi^{3/2}\Gamma(1)} = \frac{\sqrt\pi}{4\pi^{3/2}} = \frac{1}{4\pi}$
and $|x|^{-1}$: the Coulomb potential. The coefficient is finite for $0 < a < d/2$, the range in which the transform exists
as a function:

{{< sage exr-ren-ad-fourier >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
